statement: Tower A is 3 m taller than B. C is 2 m shorter than A. D is 4 m taller than C. How many metres taller is the tallest tower than the shortest?

choices.misconception: I found how much taller D is than A and stopped there.
I thought A was the tallest and found how much taller it is than B.
I thought C was the shortest, so I gave the 4 m between C and D.
I just added up the three numbers in the clues, 3, 2 and 4.

hints: Give tower B a height and work out the others.
Put all four towers on one number line by measuring each from the same starting tower. Then the tallest and shortest can be read off directly instead of guessed.
If B is 0, then A is 3, C is 1 and D is 5.

solutions.reliable: Measure from B. A is 3 m above B, C is 2 m below A, so 1 m above B, and D is 4 m above C, so 5 m above B. In order from shortest: B, C, A, D. The tallest, D, is 5 m taller than the shortest, B. The transferable idea: place everything on one line measured from a single reference point.

whyOnTest: Ordering from relative clues needs one common reference, and each partial comparison is offered as a trap.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
